cues.say: Component 4: Postgres (managed). The standard relational database: tables of rows that many users can change at once without corrupting anything. Your source of truth. You'll bring this up during version one, when you draw the basic design.
Think of it as: A shared spreadsheet that enforces its own rules. Use it for orders, payments, stock, and bookings.
Here's a real scenario. Two customers click the 9 AM Saturday slot at the tire shop at the same instant.
Without it: Booking saved, but the bay never marked taken (crash in between).
Both customers get the same bay.
With it: One transaction: mark bay taken and save booking, both or neither.
Unique rule on (bay, time) rejects the second insert.
Second customer is offered the next free slot.
Why it works: These facts must never be wrong, and the database guarantees them. A few writes a second is nothing for one database.
In the interview, say: Postgres, not Dynamodatabase: my write changes two rows together, and one database is plenty at these numbers.
A few related terms you may hear.
Transaction: Several changes succeed or fail together .
Constraint: A rule the database enforces, like unique (bay, time).
Index: A sorted lookup, so a query doesn't read every row. Every frequent query needs one.
Managed: The cloud handles backups, patches and recovery.
Dynamodatabase: Huge-scale lookups by id; clunky multi-row changes; about 1,000 writes a second per hot item.
Sharding: Splitting data across databases. Never in V1.
